title: What State AI Laws Have in Common
subtitle: Eight patterns from the text of the AI measures states have passed
body_html:
What the state AI laws have in common

We built a page from the enrolled text of each AI measure in this tracker that a state has passed, then compared them: 100 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. No two states wrote the same law. The same choices keep appearing anyway, and a business that builds to them has covered the duties that recur most often. Each pattern below names the laws that show it, and each law links to our page on it.

1. States regulate a use, not the technology

Only two states passed a broad law that reaches consequential decisions across sectors: Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. That is why a national company meets a patchwork. The question in each state is never whether you use AI. It is what you use it for.

2. The most common duty is to say it is AI

Disclosure is the single obligation that shows up most often. Chatbot operators must tell users they are not talking to a person (CA SB243, GA SB540, HI SB3001, ID S1297, ME LD1727, NY S03008, RI H7350, WA HB2225). Political advertising that uses synthetic media must carry a disclaimer (LA HB459, ME LD517, ND HB1167, TN HB1513, VT S0023). The same idea reaches health care in RI H7538 and even the bar exam in CA AB1651.

3. Children and people in crisis come first

Seven states have now passed companion chatbot laws: California, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, New York, Rhode Island and Washington. All seven require a protocol for a user who expresses suicidal thoughts or self harm. Five of them, California, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho and Washington, add specific protections for minors. California went furthest with CA SB1119, which requires a child safety risk assessment before a new chatbot launches.

4. Deepfakes are handled by extending laws already on the books

States have rarely written a new deepfake code. More often they amended what they had. Voyeurism, identity fraud, child sexual abuse material and right of publicity statutes were widened to cover synthetic images and voices (CA AB621, HI HB2137, ID H0727, LA SB42, LA SB110, MD SB8, TN HB1299, UT HB0276). These are also the laws most likely to carry criminal penalties or let the person depicted sue.

5. A qualified human has to make the call

Where the stakes are personal, legislatures keep writing the same rule: AI may assist, but it may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone (AL SB63, IA HF2635). AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician (IL HB1806, TN HB1470, CA AB489). It cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation (IL HB1859, IL SB2909), and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions (NY S07599).

6. Enforcement runs through offices that already exist

No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively (CA SB53, CO SB189, GA SB540, ID S1297, IL SB0315, NY S06953, RI H7350, TX HB149). Several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act (CT HB05222, HI SB3001, ME LD1727, TN HB1470, WA HB2225). Insurance commissioners, licensing boards and election agencies handle their own sectors. A private right to sue is the exception, and it appears mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.

7. States start with their own house, and with study

About one in five measures passed is a study committee, a commission or a resolution with no binding duty. Another group governs only the state itself: inventories of automated tools, staff training, ethics codes and procurement standards (NY S00822, TX HB2818, TX HB3512, TX SB1964, MD SB114). Both are worth watching. Study committees are where next session's bills are drafted, and rules a state writes for its own agencies tend to become the rules it later writes for vendors.

8. Frontier model laws are few, and nearly identical

Three states regulate the developers of the largest models: California (CA SB53), Illinois (IL SB0315) and New York (NY S06953, NY S08828). All three use the same frame: publish a safety framework, report critical safety incidents, and answer to the attorney general for civil penalties. They apply to a handful of companies. For everyone else they matter as a preview of the documentation large vendors will start passing down in contracts.

What this means for your business

Build to the common core and you have met the duties that recur most often. Tell people when they are dealing with AI. Keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education. If your product holds a conversation, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user. Keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet.

How to read the count. The tracker counts measures passed, which includes non binding resolutions and companion bills that passed both chambers as separate numbers, so the number of distinct statutes is lower. Patterns here come from the enrolled text of each measure, not from press coverage. Where a text could not be fully extracted, the page for that measure says so. This is reference material, not legal advice.
